title: Write three functions
task: Create `exercises/ex0_4_basics.py` (the Run command below creates a starter) with three functions: `word_count(text)` returns the number of words; `most_common_word(text)` returns the most frequent word, ignoring case; `invoice_total(items)` takes a list of `{"price": ..., "qty": ...}` dictionaries and returns the total.
hint: `text.lower().split()` gives a list of words; a dictionary can count them.
done_when: Running the file prints correct results for three examples of each function, and `./course.sh check 0.4` passes.

title: Summarize a forecast
task: Write `summarize_forecast(json_text)` that takes the JSON text of a multi-day forecast (use the `forecast` example in `ch00_json.py` as input) and returns a dictionary with the hottest day, the average maximum temperature and the list of days with rain probability above 0.5. Return a clear error string if the JSON is invalid.
hint: Catch `json.JSONDecodeError`.
done_when: It gives the right answer for the example and a readable error for `"not json"`, and `./course.sh check 0.5` passes.

title: A careful API call
task: Write `city_temperature(city)` that calls the Open-Meteo geocoding API (`https://geocoding-api.open-meteo.com/v1/search?name=<city>&count=1`), then the forecast API, and returns today's maximum temperature. Handle three failures, each with an `ERROR:` message: no network, a non-200 status and a city that isn't found.
hint: Open `https://geocoding-api.open-meteo.com/v1/search?name=Pune&count=1` in your browser first to see the JSON. The coordinates are in `results[0]`, and when no city matches, there's no `results` key at all.
done_when: It works for three real cities, returns sensible errors for "Xyzzyqq" and for a wrong URL, and `./course.sh check 0.6` passes.

title: Expense report tool

hint: Python's `csv.DictReader` reads each row as a dictionary.
done_when: The JSON report is correct for your sample, including a `skipped_rows` count, and the program never crashes on a bad row.

title: Comprehensions

done_when: `./course.sh check P.2` passes.

title: A class of your own

done_when: `./course.sh check P.3` passes.

title: Decorators
task: Write a `tool` decorator that registers a function in `TOOLS` under its name, with its docstring as the description, and returns the function unchanged. Then write `count_calls`, a decorator that records in a `calls` dictionary how many times each function was called.
hint: Section 5. A decorator is a function that takes a function and returns a function.
done_when: `./course.sh check P.4` passes.

title: Find the bugs

title: Single call, workflow or agent?
chapter: Chapter 1: What an Agent Is (and Isn't)

hint: Ask "Could I draw the flowchart before the task starts?"

title: Tokens and cost
chapter: Chapter 1: What an Agent Is (and Isn't)
task: A conversation has a 2,000-token system prompt and grows by 500 tokens per turn. Estimate the total input tokens sent over 10 turns, remembering that each call resends the whole history.
hint: The input for turn *n* is 2,000 + 500 × *n*.
done_when: You have a number and can explain why agent costs grow faster than linearly with conversation length.

chapter: Chapter 1: What an Agent Is (and Isn't)
task: Run `ch01_summarize.py`. Then change the system prompt to "Explain like I am 10 years old" and compare the output and the token counts.

hint: Models often wrap JSON in a Markdown code fence (a line of three backticks before and after) even when asked not to. Take the text between the first `{` and the last `}` before parsing, and wrap the parse in `try/except` so a bad reply doesn't crash the run.
done_when: It handles all five emails, and you've noted which email a fixed workflow handled badly.

title: Where does the agent go?

task: Take the support-email workflow from section 1.6 and write a one-page design note: which emails would need the steps to change at run time, which tools an agent would need (name at least four), what information it would need in front of it at each step, and what could go wrong if the agent had those tools. done_when: The note names concrete tools and risks and includes a cost comparison. Keep it; you'll revisit it in Capstone 1. This note is the Design stage of the lifecycle in section 1.10.

title: Which kind of agent?

title: Who wrote this?

title: Run and trace

task: Add a `percent_change(old, new)` tool without changing the structure of the round-trip code. Then ask "Revenue went from 84,213 to 97,400. task: Extend `verify` to catch two more failures: a quotation (text in quotation marks) that doesn't appear in the cited evidence, and a claim cited to the wrong source (the cited evidence doesn't contain any of the sentence's key words). When verification fails, ask the model to revise once with the list of problems, then verify again. Measure on 10 questions how many answers pass verification before and after revision.

title: Evaluate the routers

done_when: The resumed job finishes without repeating any finished step or model call, and the report shows which model ran each step.

title: Pick the topology

done_when: Each system has a topology from section 21.1, a reason, and a limit with a number.

title: Write the contracts
task: Write the brief template and the result schema for a handoff from a lead to a "competitor pricing" specialist. The lead needs prices for five named products from three competitors, with sources and the date each price was seen.

done_when: A test shows all three failures reach the lead as `ERROR:` results without an exception, and a second attempt after a contract error succeeds.

title: A team of A2A agents
task: Publish the Chapter 5 to-do agent as a second A2A agent, next to the analyst from section 21.7. Give it its own agent card (name, description and one skill with examples) and reuse `AgentLoopExecutor` and `build_app` from `ch21_a2a_server.py`. Then build a coordinator that reads both cards and gets one tool per remote agent from `a2a_tool`. done_when: Both cards print, the coordinator delegates once to each agent, and `tasks.json` contains the new task.

title: A mixed team
task: Add the A2A analyst from section 21.7 to the demo team as a remote member, `Agent("remote_analyst", ..., remote_url=url)`, next to the local analyst and the checker. Ask a question both analysts can answer, have the lead compare their answers, and send any disagreement to the checker.
hint: `start_local_server` from `ch21_a2a_client.py` runs the remote analyst in the same process.
done_when: The board shows tasks for the local analyst, the remote analyst and the checker, the final result names the evidence it relied on, and you've compared the team's tokens with the local analyst's alone.

title: Where does the team pay?
task: Use `simulated_runs` and `coordination_report` from `ch21_coordination.py` on the multi-part questions, and sweep the tool latency over 0.5, 1, 1.5, 2, 3 and 4 seconds. For each latency, record the p95 of one agent that runs its tool calls one after another, of one agent that runs them at the same time (`parallel_tools=True`), and of the lead with workers, plus the team's extra cost per task. Find the smallest tool latency at which the team beats the first single agent on p95, and say whether it ever beats the second. Then use `failure_propagation` to find how many workers a team with a planning and a synthesis step (`lead_steps=2`) can have, at 97% per step with failures contained, before the chance that every part is right falls below 80%, without retries and with one retry per worker.
hint: The simulator uses virtual time, so the whole sweep takes a few seconds. For the second part, increase `n` until `p_task` drops below 0.8.
done_when: You have a six-row table, the crossover latency, a yes or no for the parallel single agent and the two worker counts, and a sentence on what each result means for the team's design.

title: Model or code?
chapter: Chapter 22: Hybrid Architectures: Probabilistic Intelligence, Deterministic Control
task: For an expense-report assistant, decide who owns each decision, the model or code, and why: (a) the category of an expense from its receipt; (b) whether an expense is over the daily meal limit; (c) converting a receipt in euros to dollars; (d) the explanation sent to an employee whose expense is rejected; (e) whether a manager must approve; (f) spotting a receipt that looks altered.
done_when: Each decision has an owner and a reason, and where the model owns it, you've named the check or evaluation that keeps it honest.

title: Find the holes
chapter: Chapter 22: Hybrid Architectures: Probabilistic Intelligence, Deterministic Control
task: A team built a refund agent with one prompt: "You are a refund assistant. Refunds are allowed within 30 days, up to $100 without approval. Use the refund tool." The tool takes `order_id` and `amount`. List five ways this system could refund the wrong amount, the wrong order or the wrong person, and for each, the control from this chapter that prevents it.
done_when: You have five distinct failures, each paired with a specific control.

title: Follow the five paths
chapter: Chapter 22: Hybrid Architectures: Probabilistic Intelligence, Deterministic Control
task: Run `ch22_guarded.py` twice: approve the refund that asks for approval the first time and decline it the second. For each of the five requests, name the states it went through and the line of code that decided each transition.
done_when: You can explain every line of the log, including why the $5,000 request didn't refund $5,000.

title: Change the policy, not the code
chapter: Chapter 22: Hybrid Architectures: Probabilistic Intelligence, Deterministic Control
task: Move `POLICY` into `refund_policy.json` with a version number, load it at start-up, and record the policy version in every case's log. Then add a rule without touching `decide`'s structure: orders over $300 are refundable only for `damaged` or `wrong_item`.

done_when: Tests cover day 30 and day 31, $100 and $100.01, and the new rule, and each case's log names the policy version that decided it.

title: Attack the workflow
chapter: Chapter 22: Hybrid Architectures: Probabilistic Intelligence, Deterministic Control
task: Write six messages that try to break the workflow: an inflated amount, another customer's order, an order id the customer never mentions, an instruction to skip approval, a request with no valid reason, and a message asking for a voucher. Run each through `handle` with a model that follows the attacker's lead as far as it can.

title: A guarded SQL analyst
chapter: Chapter 22: Hybrid Architectures: Probabilistic Intelligence, Deterministic Control
task: Rebuild the Chapter 8 analyst's `run_query` as a hybrid: the model writes SQL, and code decides whether it runs. Use SQLite's `set_authorizer` to allow only reads of the shop's tables, add a row limit, and inject the business definitions (such as revenue) into the system prompt from a definitions file rather than trusting the model to know them.
hint: The authorizer is called for every action the SQL would take; return `sqlite3.SQLITE_DENY` for anything that isn't a read of an allowed table or a function you allow.

title: Screen or API?
task: For each task, choose an API, an MCP server, a database export or a computer-use agent, and say why: (a) updating 500 product prices in a store that has a REST API; (b) downloading monthly invoices from a supplier portal with no API; (c) checking that your own sign-up page works on every release; (d) copying data between two internal tools, one of which has an export; (e) filing expense reports in a desktop application from 2009.

Then sign in again, as the person would, and run the queue again.

chapter: Chapter 24: Skills, Frameworks and Agent Runtimes
task: Run `ch24_managed_agent.py` against the real API. Ask it for a revenue report that it saves as a CSV in its sandbox. Deny one bash command and watch how it adapts, then lower the session budget until it stops with `budget_reached`.

chapter: Chapter 24: Skills, Frameworks and Agent Runtimes

chapter: Chapter 24: Skills, Frameworks and Agent Runtimes
task: The regression gate in section 24.10 checks that a new skill version still does its job, but it doesn't notice that 1.3.0 can suddenly send email. task: For each agent, say whether it has private data, untrusted content and a way out, and if it has all three, which leg you'd remove and how: (a) a coding agent that reads GitHub issues and can push to the repository; (b) a travel assistant that reads your email and books flights; (c) a research agent that fetches web pages and writes to a shared memory; (d) an internal HR chatbot that answers from the employee handbook only; (e) a sales agent that reads CRM records and sends emails to customers.

task: Pick one agent you built (or your capstone). For each of the ten OWASP agentic risks in section 25.9, write one line: how it could happen to *this* agent, and which defense you have. Mark any risk you haven't covered.

done_when: A test shows the planner never receives an invite's description, the external invite creates no task, and a genuine internal invite does.

title: Red team your agent
task: Build a throwaway `redteam/` folder (its own notes and its own Git repository, never your real ones) and plant six attacks: in a file name, in a note's text, in a Git commit message, in a web page (serve it from a small "simulated internet" MCP server with a `fetch` tool that logs every URL) and two **exfiltration** attempts that ask the agent to read `secret.md` and send it to a site, one unknown and one on your allow-list. task: For each action, name the user, the agent and the service, the scopes the token needs, and whether it needs a step-up: (a) a calendar agent books a meeting room for Priya; (b) a finance agent pays a supplier invoice of $12,000; (c) a coding agent opens a pull request in the team's repository; (d) a research subagent reads three internal wiki pages for its lead; (e) an HR agent reads an employee's salary history to answer the employee's own question.
done_when: Every action has all three identities, minimal scopes, and a step-up decision with a reason.

task: Serve the order tools as a small HTTP API with Starlette that accepts `Authorization: Bearer <token>` and checks it with `authorize`, audience `orders-api`.
